speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the few years I have had the privilege of serving as a Member of Parliament in this Chamber there have been debates of great importance. One of those debates I recall so vividly was on the future of Canada itself and the question of the referendum in Quebec and whether Quebec would separate from Canada.
Another was one in which we talked about patriation of the Constitution and the implementation of a Charter of Rights that would put the rights of Canadians above those of any legislator, including those of us here in this Chamber.
Today, I believe we are in a debate that has very important, if not equally important, consequences for the future of our country and for the future of Canadians.
We are debating spending. We are debating a Budget. However, what makes this debate unique is the direction that this Budget has taken and the direction of this debate. We are seeing across from us a Government which has made the deficit its priority. We on this side of the House do not disagree that Canada's national deficit is of grave concern to all Canadians. The question, however, is: How does one decide to go about dealing with this particular problem?
We have two alternatives before us which I suggest to all Members of this House will determine the economic future of this country for years to come. We have before us a Budget which talks of the powers of the marketplace, the laissez-faire concept that corporations should be able to do as they wish. This is the concept of foreign takeovers, where Canadian firms are up for sale, even those companies we have nurtured through public money. I am referring to such companies such as Connaught, Lumonics, companies at the leading edge of technology. Yet we have said that they can be taken over by foreigners with the possibility that what we have built up here in Canada might forever be lost to us as Canadians.
We have a Budget which says that the future of Canada does not really lie in our hands. We can turn control of Canadian companies over to foreign corpora-
Borrowing Authority
tions. As one Minister said, "let it happen, it is good for us".
These are some of the prospects we are dealing with, Madam Speaker, from the other side of the House. What have they done in terms of attempting to cope with the deficit? This again is a way we can determine the economic future of this country, for a Budget is not only a means of raising revenue, it is a way of declaring where a Government is actually putting its priorities. It is a way of determining not what the rhetoric says, but where they are prepared to spend their money. Where have they put their money?
It is pretty obvious to us, Madam Speaker, that the rhetoric is not matched by their actions. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the House of Commons just three days ago on April 28 said: "While Canada is wrestling with a very serious fiscal problem the Government is standing up for Canadians." These are the Canadians he has stood up for: seniors, who are losing part of their old age security; parents, whose family allowances are being cut; and our children who want to go to universities or community colleges. Transfer payments to the provinces are being cut. What about our younger children? The Government has reneged on its promise to create 200,000 new child care spaces. What about the homeless? CMHC has had $49 million cut from its budget. What about the sick? Transfer payments for health care to the provinces have been cut and as for the unemployed, payments to the unemployed in this country have been cut.
Nothing has been done to help the one million Canadian children who live below the poverty level. The three million Canadians now living below the poverty level can find no succour in this Budget, not one new program to help them. What has been done to help the five million Canadians who are functionally illiterate and will not be able to have full opportunities in the job market in the future? Nothing.
Look at Canada's disadvantaged regions. Regional development funding has been cut by $240 million for next year and by $400 million for the years thereafter. The Regional Economic Development Agreements have expired; they expired on March 31 to the tune of $1.6 billion and have not been renewed.

May 2, 1989
Borrowing Authority
This Government is allowing the cut-back of key transportation facilities to the more distant regions of Canada: VIA Rail, Air Canada. How can these regions be strong if the communications with the rest of Canada are not built upon? We are penalizing those who have to go the farthest in this country with the gas tax. Again, that does not hit those people in the big urban regions who have public transportation as hard. It hits the people who have to drive long distances to their jobs and to market their goods. These are the people of Canada's regions.
In cutting back on military bases, again in the regions of Canada, we are insensitive to the needs of those particular communities. We are prepared to decimate them. The Minister yesterday in this House said, Madam Speaker, that as far as Grand Prairie is concerned, they are going to look at new ways to train our military forces. They are going to contract these services out. This is the absurd level to which this Government is prepared to take its right wing Tory policies. They are going to privatize the Canadian Armed Forces.
What is going to happen to the regions of Canada that are so dependent on tourism and on the service sector as opposed to the manufacturing sector? Who will this new goods and services tax prejudice the most? It will be those regions that are dependent on these sectors I have just spoken of where the new taxes are going to apply in a way they do not now that will hit every aspect of those economies without any thought for the fact that these regions of Canada deserve a break. Canada's regions are critical to the economic future of all of us. We as Canadians cannot be strong if our regions are not strong and if Canadians from all regions do not have economic opportunities.
Who else have they hit? Our homeowners. Tax on construction materials has gone from eight per cent to nine per cent. It will increase the average cost of a house in Canada by about $500. Add to that the new UI benefits that will have to be assumed by employers and workers. So you can add on another couple of hundred dollars to the cost of a house.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) I know must feel chagrined. There was a cut from his budget for overseas development. It was one of the biggest whacks taken out of our possibility for spending to create the type of world we want, a world that is humane, where neighbours look after neighbours. Until we realize that unless we can bring the rest of the world to higher standards of living, to higher standards of health care, to literacy, to education, to shelter, we Canadians will not fulfil our role as humanitarians and
world leaders. We even jeopardize our long-term economic future.
Nothing in this Budget helps our cultural industries, the industries that help us to define ourselves as Canadians.
In terms of going about the task, Madam Speaker, of building a type of industrial infrastructure we want here in Canada, what has happened in terms of the education and training to which this Government has paid lip service, to which the Government's own commissioner, de Grandpre, said we need much more spending and readjustment on training to cope with the new economic realities and to protect us from the ravages of the free trade agreement with the United States. On this the Budget is silent.
In terms of research and development, to which this Government has committed itself time after time, there are no incentives. Incentives that have previously been in the Income Tax Act to encourage innovation in Canada and to encourage incorporation of the new technologies into Canadian goods have been removed. There is no new tax on corporations, as de Grandpre suggested, to deal with the training requirements, to deal with the investment in our human capital, which is so critical to our economic future and so critical to fairness here in Canada.
We should look at our small businesses, which are the lifeblood of Canadian job creation, and the training of entrepreneurs, which is the heart of many communities. What has happened? John Bulloch, friend of the Conservative Government, said: "I call this Budget a tax tidal wave that is going to wash out consumer spending and business activity." The Government has increased the small business tax. The burden of unemployment insurance, which has now been privatized, will be about $2.9 billion falling on the private sector. The goods and services tax will add another nine per cent. The federal sales tax, the most regressive you can imagine and one that is harmful to manufacturing everywhere in Canada, has been increased from 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent.
Then the construction tax I mentioned, which impinges on small business. Even if our businesses want to diversify into the regions, the first thing they are going to hit, apart from decreased transportation facilities, is the additional tax on telecommunications. If they need help to get established, do they go any more to the FBDB whose funding has been cut by $13 million? If one is looking to aerospace, which is a leader among Canadian industries on the world scene, one would see a cut of $25 million.
May 2, 1989

Yes, one can say that we have a deficit. That is what the Government has been saying through every one of its Members. They are saying that every cut is justified because we have a deficit. They do not tell us that the deficit has doubled in the four years that they have been in office controlling the economy. There are alternatives that they could have undertaken in dealing with the deficit, if they had not been such terrible financial managers. They have justified the Budget to us on the basis that it reduces the deficit. Last year the deficit was $28.9 billion. This year it is $30.5 billion. They have not decreased it, it has gone up.
How have they gone about coping with the deficit problem? They have done it in a right wing, machiavellian fashion on the backs of the disadvantaged. They have done it by cutting programs directed at the homeless, the poor, the sick, the weak, children, the illiterate and the regions. They have also done it on the backs of the average and the poor taxpayer. Since the Government has come into office it has increased the taxes of a family living at the poverty line by a full 60 per cent. They have taken the middle income family with income in the neighbourhood of $40,000 to $50,000 and over their tenure have increased the taxes paid by that family by 30 per cent. Taxes on the families in the $100,000 income range have gone up only 8 per cent. The share of income taxes paid in Canada by corporations has declined steadily under the Government.
What we have seen is an attempt to deal with the deficit, but it is being done on the backs of the poor and middle income Canadians. They are doing it by taking further from the programs that create social and economic justice for those least able and equipped to deal with it. They are doing it with all the advantages, all the breaks directed at the highest paid people in our society, high income Canadians and our major corporations.
I said when I started my remarks that this is an historic debate. It is a watershed in terms of Canadian political history as to where we are going. Unfortunately, the Government has another four years before it has to put its case to the people again. However, I suspect that
Borrowing Authority
many of its Members over the next couple of years will want to cross the floor to join us. They will want to do that because their constituents know that the way they are tackling the problem of the deficit is not only ill-managed but ill-conceived in terms of fairness.
Members opposite have a mandate. If they carry it out the way they have set it out in the Budget we will see Thatcherism run amok. The rich will benefit at the expense of the poor. We will see a two-class Canada. We will see rich individuals and poor individuals, rich regions and poor regions. We will see the disadvantaged remain disadvantaged, those who with a bit of help and understanding from the federal Government could become productive players on the Canadian economic scene. We can see these people being put down further by the Government when in fact it had the option to invest in them and make them full-class Canadians, full-class players in our economy.
We are seeing a meanness and a pettiness which accompany the total incompetence the Government has demonstrated in dealing with our national economic problems. This is a watershed in our economic history. It will be a watershed in our social history as well. The Government is taking it out on the backs of the poor. I want people to think about this. Is this truly the direction we wish to go in?
I believe that Canadians are fair. As my Leader said just a few minutes ago in what I believe was an historic speech, Canadians are prepared to sacrifice, providing that they perceive that sacrifice to be fair and providing that they see it as giving benefit to those who most need it. The Budget meets none of those criteria. It meets none of the criteria for helping to build a strong economy for Canada's benefit. It is a Budget which turns us more and more over to the foreign elements that are taking control of Canada to an even greater extent.
In conclusion, we Liberals on this side of the House ask Canadians to ask themselves these questions: When will the Government stand up for Canada? When will it stand up for them? When will it be fair?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would be delighted if I were in government to set forth a completely alternative agenda in terms of what could be done. The first thing we would not do is what the Tories have done.
Let us consider the concept of wealth creation in Canada. Madam Speaker, do you think we can produce a strong economy for Canadians in the future if our key Canadian industries are going to be turned over lock, stock and barrel to any foreign corporation that wants to buy them out? Since Investment Canada was reconstituted by the Tory Government, it has received 606 applications for takeovers of Canadian enterprises by foreign firms. Every one has been approved. It is nothing but a rubber stamp operation.
Why do foreign companies want to take over Canadian companies? It is because they can get at our research and development. They can get at our technologies. They can take the profits out of Canada for reinvestment in their home countries.
In terms of creating additional wealth in Canada we would emphasize our human resources. Japan, for example, as I am sure the Secretary of State well knows, spends twice as much per capita in educating its human resources as does Canada. If we do not have an intelligent, informed, 21st century knowledge level of human resources in Canada, how can we compete on the world markets? This is the difference between the Tories and the Liberals. We look on education. We look on bolstering the handicapped and training them. We look on curing the sick not as a privilege that should be the subject of deficit cuts. These are investments in human resources. So there is a fundamental difference of philosophy between us.
In terms of raising taxes, we would not have, as the Tories have done over the last five years of their fiscal management of Canada, increased by 60 per cent the taxes payable by a Canadian couple with two children whose total poverty level income is $23,500. We would not have increased the taxes borne by middle-income Canadians over that same period, with the same type of family but with an income of about $45,000, by 30 per cent. We would not have done it in a regressive way-through sales taxes, which hit the poorest in the most excessive manner.
May 2, 1989

The sales tax applies to everything a person consumes. If you are spending all of your money simply to live, you are paying a far greater percentage of your income in sales taxes than if you are a rich person who has the discretion as to whether to invest or to spend.
The top level of income taxes have gone consistently down. We have a Government that has granted a $100,000 capital gains exemption to the rich. We have a Government that says if you buy a condominium in Florida and put your money there, you do not have to pay gains on the taxes here in Canada. That condominium in Florida is not creating jobs for Canadians. We have a Government that is not prepared to invest in the industries of the future. They look on tax incentives for research and development for new technologies as an expenditure. We know that we cannot compete in the world marketplace unless we are going to spend money as other governments do, as other nations do to create the highest level of technological development, the highest level of research here in Canada.
What they have done, in a nutshell, is they have given up our possibilities of being competitive in a more fiercely competitive world. They have denied us this right with this Budget. Secondly, they have taken the money from the weakest people in Canada. They have left the richest groups, the most privileged groups, with the lowest tax burdens. They have used the most regressive form of taxation on the backs of the poor in order to deal with this deficit, a deficit I cannot for the life of me understand. This right wing Government is so pre-occupied with cutting government spending, yet it has increased Government spending over its five years to inordinate levels. It is a Government that has totally mismanaged the economy. In spite of the fact that its revenues have gone up 60 per cent during its term of office, it has not been able to reduce that deficit.
The deficit today is $1.6 billion higher than it was last year. This is as a result of incompetence and bungling. It demonstrates a lack of priorities and a lack of investment in our future. And in every one of these Budget cuts to Canada's disadvantaged groups the Government has lied to us. They said they would not cut in any of these areas, but they have cut them to the bone.
Borrowing Authority
Canadians have been misled. When Canadians start to realize where their true economic future lies, where fairness and justice lie, they are going to revolt, and we will never have seen one of a greater magnitude in this country.
I suspect the Secretary of State for External Affairs feels chagrined when he attends international councils representing Canada and he has to admit that we have sacrificed our commitment to the poorest people, to the poorest regions in the world. I have great sympathy for you, sir; those of us on this side of the House do. We know you fought to keep those programs, because you are a decent man.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 PRPOSED AMENDMENT-DELETION OF ARTICLE 59
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should initiate an amendment to the Constitution Act, 1982 to delete article 59, which restricts the rights of Anglo-Quebecers to education in their own language.
He said: Madam Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to assure that English-speaking Quebecers have the same constitutional rights to education in their language as francophone Canadians outside Quebec have in their language. In other words, the purpose of the motion is to ensure that there is equality with respect to language rights for English-speaking Quebecers and Frenchspeaking Canadians outside Quebec. That is the purpose of the motion.
That equality does not exist at the present time. It does not exist because of Article 59 of the Constitution Act, 1982. Let me explain.
When the Constitution Act, 1982 was tabled in the House in 1981, Article 59 was not part of it. It did not exist. At that time, minority language rights with respect to education were governed entirely by Article 23 of the Constitution Act, 1982.
Let me read that Article. It states:
23(1) Citizens of Canada
(a)	whose first language learned and still understood is that of the English or French linguistic minority population of the province in which they reside,. . .
They have the right "to have their children receive primary and secondary school instruction in that language in that province." In addition those citizens.
(b)	who have received their primary school instruction in Canada in English or French and reside in a province where the language in which they received that instruction is the language of the English or French linguistic minority population of the province-have the right to have their children receive primary and secondary school instruction in that language in that province will also have that right.
Article 23(l)(a) says that an anglophone in the Province of Quebec whose language first learned and still understood was English, has the right to send his children to English schools if and when he has children. It said the same thing for Francophones outside Quebec. If their mother tongue was French and they still understood French they had the right to send their children to French schools in any province in Canada, if that was the situation.
The article also says that even though a person's mother tongue was not French or English but that person had received his primary education in French or English, he also had the right to send his children to those French or English schools. That was the situation when the Constitution Act, 1982 was tabled in the House in 1981. While that Article had some imperfections, which I will discuss later, it was a good article. I supported it, as I supported the entire Constitution with great enthusiasm. I supported the Charter of Rights and the repatriation of the Constitution. I supported the amending clause.
However, in the later months of 1981, following a decision of the Supreme Court, there was a hastily called federal-provincial conference to deal with the decision of that court. Several changes were made to the Constitution Act as presented to the House of Commons. One of those changes was the famous notwithstanding clause. It was added. However, also added at that time was Article 59. It suspended to paragraph 23(l)(a). That is the paragraph I just read that states that if the first language learned and still understood is French or English, one has the right to have one's children educated in the minority language. Article 59 states that paragraph 21(l)(a):
May 2, 1989

-shall come into force in respect of Quebec on a day to be fixed by proclamation issued by the Queen or the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada.
It went on to say that a proclamation under that subsection could only be issued where authorized by the Legislative Assembly or Government of Quebec.
While I voted against it, what the Parliament did was suspend the right of English-speaking Quebecers to have education in their own language if their mother tongue was English. It left with them the right to have their children educated in English if they had attended primary education in English, but it took away the first basis for access to minority language education. We ended up with a situation where Articles 23(a) and (b) apply to Francophones outside Quebec but only Article 23(b) applied to Anglophones inside Quebec. I spoke against this provision at the time. I felt that I could never accept the entrenchment in the Constitution of such an inequity, an inequity where Anglophones of Quebec in a constitutional sense would be treated different from Francophones outside of Quebec.
What are the consequences of that? I will refer to my own children, as I have done so before on the record. I had my children educated in the French language in Quebec because I wanted them to be totally bilingual. My son had all his primary education in French. When the day comes for him to have children and send them to school, he will have no constitutional right, despite the fact that his mother tongue is English, to send his children to an English school. He may want to send them to a French school, but he loses the right to send his children to an English school because he did not do his primary education in English. He was an Anglophone but did his primary education in French, as many Anglophones do these days in Quebec.
What is the other significance to this particular clause? I know of a case where a man from a foreign country came to Canada when he was in Grade 2. He entered the Anglophone system of education in Quebec in Grade 2 and went through to Grade 7. When he had children he tried to take advantage of that Section of the Constitution to send his children to an English school. The ruling in Quebec was that one must do all of one's primary education in English, and six out of seven years was not good enough.
Constitution Act
Article 59 was inserted into the Constitution at the last minute, along with several other changes that are better known than Article 59. At that time I objected and asked for reasons why this was being done, especially since all political Parties in the House had stood for equality of treatment with respect to Anglophones and Francophones. That was the basis of the report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism submitted to Mr. Pearson.
I asked for a reason. No sound reason has ever been given to me. No one has ever stood up to justify that article. It was inferred that that change was necessary in order to have the Constitution Act, 1982 accepted by the provinces and the federal Parliament. It was insinuated or inferred that if we did not make these changes the whole package would be defeated.
I could never accept that. As a matter of fact, I have not found out to this day who really asked for that change. We know that certain provinces asked for the notwithstanding clause, but I could never find out who asked for that particular change. It was certainly not the Parti Quebecois Government in Quebec because it was not interested in the issue at all. It was opposed to the whole initiative.
Some have said to me in later years, following 1982, that that clause was necessary in order to protect the French language. I was told that we must protect the French language in Quebec.
I have been in Parliament for 23 years. I have always been strongly in favour of measures to protect and promote the French language. Whenever there has been a violation of Francophone rights, whether in Saskatchewan, Alberta or Ontario, I have taken the side of those Francophones and fought for their rights. In the early days when I first came here, most of the infractions were on that side.
I am in favour of protecting and promoting the French language in Quebec and throughout Canada. However, it is not protected and promoted with this kind of measure. I see absolutely no relationship between a clause that disallows anglophones from seeking education in their own language and the protection of the French language and culture. It has never been demonstrated that this provision will in fact have that effect.

May 2, 1989
Constitution Act
I also submit very strongly that one does not protect one set of rights by suppressing other rights. Racial rights, language rights, or sexual equality rights are not protected by suppressing the rights of others. Again, this provision seems to be attempting to do that. It is not well thought out. The underlying thought behind it is that if the rights of anglophones are restricted, perhaps something will be done to strengthen the rights of francophones in Quebec.
Despite this restriction on anglophone rights to education in their own language, a great percentage of anglophones in the province of Quebec are seeking education in French for their children. The immersion courses in Montreal are packed to the limit. At the schools in my area, parents have to line up days in advance to get their children into the immersion programs. Of course, immersion programs are programs in English schools in which nearly everything is taught in French. As I said, there is a great demand for those courses. In addition to that, the program for teaching French in non-immersion English schools has been greatly improved since the days when I went to school in the province, with the result that young Anglo-Quebec-ers are very bilingual today. As a matter of fact, recent reports published by the Province of Quebec have shown that young anglophones in Quebec are now more bilingual than young francophones. This is surprising, because it was always the reverse in the past.
The provision in Article 59 is the result of misguided logic. As I said before, one language is not protected, enhanced, or promoted by suppressing another. We hear other arguments from time to time that attempt to justify this kind of provision. We hear that it is necessary to protect the French language in Quebec, something I have always admitted, and that in any case, English is not threatened in Canada. One hears that argument quite often.
First, I admit that the French language and culture is under threat in Quebec and in Canada, because francophones are a population of about six million to eight million people, though I forget the exact figures, surrounded by a sea of anglophones in North America. While the English language is of course not threatened in North America outside Quebec, it is threatened and has been threatened for several years now in Quebec.
The English-speaking community in Quebec is a dwindling community. Many measures such as Article 59 have discouraged young Quebecers, even though they are bilingual, and members of the community have been leaving in great numbers. Great numbers of graduating students from McGill University, Concordia University, and Bishop's University are leaving the province because they feel they are being harassed with measure after measure that restricts or suppresses their language rights. While the English language community is not threatened in Canada, it feels threatened in the province of Quebec, and this has been documented in the reports of the Official Languages Commissioner.
When people use that argument, they should be clear about it. Let us not confuse what is happening in Quebec with what is happening in all of Canada. Let us not have the suggestion that those who want to speak English can go to Ontario or Alberta. My family is fifth generation Anglo-Quebecer; my home is Quebec, and I have no intention of leaving Quebec. I want my full rights in that province, as I stand for the full rights of francophones outside Quebec.
Another argument we hear is that despite Article 59, certain sections of Bill 101 and Bill 178, the Englishspeaking community in Quebec is still the best treated minority in Canada. That was true for many, many years, but it is no longer true. It is true that there is a series of anglophone institutions in the province of Quebec, including universities and schools, but over the years the English-speaking community built those institutions itself. It was a very large community in the province.
The fact is that the threat against anglophones now is in the form of restrictive laws. There has been attempt after attempt, both provincially and federally, including Article 59, which went in the direction of restricting their rights. That cannot be accepted.
On the other hand, there has been a slow improvement in francophone rights outside Quebec. The constitutional entrenchment of certain rights has improved the situation. While we have seen an improvement in francophone rights outside Quebec, we have seen a cutting away of the rights of anglophones in the province of Quebec.
I think my time is coming to an end. I simply want to remind Hon. Members that this motion provides that the Government initiate an amendment to the Constitution Act of 1982 to delete Article 59, which restricts the rights of Anglo-Quebeckers to education in their own language. I know that other Hon. Members will say that

francophones outside Quebec have the full constitutional rights of Article 23, but their implementation is very slow and difficult. I support them in that plea and agree with them. I have seen what has happened in certain towns and cities in Canada in which there has been reluctance on the part of certain communities to carry out the rights mentioned in Article 23. However, I want their support in this motion.
I will be listening very closely in this debate to hear what Hon. Members will say, and I will be listening very closely to hear how they justify a provision like Article 59, which clearly provides that one group, the anglophones in Quebec, should not have certain rights while those rights are available to another group in all other provinces of Canada. I urge the House to take this motion seriously.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) for his interest in this matter and for the research he has done. It is a matter that really is a challenge to all of us to resolve.
The Hon. Member has proposed that Parliament should initiate an amendment to delete Article 59 of the Charter. Article 59 provides an exemption for Quebec from one of the bases for demanding minority language education rights in that province. Article 59 also provides a special unilateral executive amending procedure that allows the repeal of Article 59 but only at the time of the coming into force of the "first language learned and still understood" clause in respect of Quebec. That coming into force can only occur when authorized by the Legislative Assembly or the Government of Quebec.
I should point out that since Article 59 provides a special procedure for its own repeal, a procedure that is dependent upon a prior initiative by the Legislative Assembly or Government of Quebec, it would be inappropriate to initiate an amendment in this House. However, I should like to take this opportunity to explain why two bases for demanding minority language education rights were included in the Constitution and why only one applies in the case of Quebec.
Quebec's Bill 101 sought to grandfather everyone in the Quebec English-speaking school system at the time of its adoption in 1977, but to restrict access to English
Constitution Act
schools in the future. This was because the rapidly declining birth rate among francophone Quebeckers would make it neessary to integrate immigrants into the French-speaking community if it were to maintain its relative demographic strength. Therefore, Bill 101 only provided the right to English language education to the children of Canadian citizens who had received their primaiy education in Quebec in English, a clause known as the Quebec clause.
In the interests of the mobility of Canadian citizens, the Quebec Government said that it would be willing to extend this Quebec clause to a Canada clause, that is, the right would apply to the children of Canadian citizens who had received their primary education in Canada rather than only in Quebec.
However, because the other provinces had been far less expansive, historically, than Quebec in the treatment of linguistic minorities, and because in a number of provinces the right to education in the minority language was eliminated or sharply curtailed at one point or another, a considerable proportion of Canadian Francophone parents living outside Quebec could not receive their primary instruction in French. Thus, the Canada clause would create rights for almost all Anglophones living in Quebec while a high number of Francophones outside Quebec would have no right whatsoever.
In these circumstances, the federal Government devised the "first language learned and still understood" clause to provide the right for the children of Canadian Francophones who were not allowed to be educated in primary schools in their own tongue.
When it was decided by Prime Minister Trudeau to impose Section 23, the minority language education rights, on the National Assembly without its consent in 1981, he determined that the Canada clause, which Quebec had offered on the basis of reciprocity to the other provinces, should apply to Quebec because all other provinces accepted it.
However, the other provinces, recognizing that historical policies would effectively limit the application of the Canada clause to their own Francophones, agreed to be bound by the alternate right based on the "first language learned and still understood" clause.

May 2, 1989
Constitution Act
The same historical problems did not arise in Quebec and did not require the corrective of this alternative right. Furthermore, this alternative right could undermine Quebec immigration policy. It was for this reason that the Government, of which the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace was a member, did not impose the "first language learned and still understood" clause in Quebec. That is why it would be extremely inappropriate for us to ratify this amendment.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise this afternoon as a Member of this House who had the honour of participating in the debates on the constitutional amendments in 1981 and of sitting on the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada. I want to emphasize that in private Members' hour my remarks are personal and that I am not speaking on behalf of my caucus colleagues. I speak on my own behalf on this very important question.
I remember well the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) who spoke with strength and conviction at the time the Section 59 provision was before the House. He did not propose an amendment to Section 59 respecting the constitutional resolution which was before the House in November of 1981. I do not know why he did not propose that amendment at the time his Government was in power. Certainly one could say that it is never too late.
There is a logical inconsistency in what is suggested here. Under Section 59 of the Constitution Act there is a special provision with respect to Quebec. The Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace is proposing an amendment under Section 43 of the Constitution Act, 1982. That amendment would only apply to Quebec and could only take effect if the National Assembly in the Province of Quebec agreed to the change.
If the National Assembly of the Province of Quebec were prepared to agree to the change proposed by my hon. friend from Notre-Dame-de-Grace, it could move forward under Section 59 of the Constitution Act because under that section a proclamation can be issued where it is agreed upon by the National Assembly of the Province of Quebec. Obviously, if the National Assembly of the Province of Quebec wanted to proceed in that manner, it could do so.
\Translation]
Madam Speaker, if we, in the Parliament of Canada, in this House, are prepared to accept Quebec's distinct society, we must ask ourselves how is Quebec distinct? If it is not its linguistic and cultural characteristics that make it distinct, I do not know what does. Personally, I believe that, ultimately, Quebec's National Assembly must decide what measures are necessary to protect that specificity, Quebec's distinct society.
That is why, Madam Speaker, I support the principles of Quebec's Bill 101. That is why I oppose and speak against the proposal of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand). He suggests the English language, the Anglophone minority in Quebec, is at risk. But it is not so, Madam Speaker.
Even the Official Languages Commissioner, in his annual report that was tabled a few weeks ago, says no for the first time. The English language, the Englishspeaking minority in Quebec are not threatened.
My colleague recognizes that the French language is threatened in Canada and, as a Member for British Columbia, I assure you that if Francophone parents had the same rights as Anglophone parents in Quebec, they would be very happy. That is to say, Madam Speaker, that our priority should be to make section 23 a reality everywhere in Canada to protect the rights of Francophone minorities outside Quebec, rights that still do not exist in the other provinces of Canada.
Madam Speaker, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Richelieu (Mr. Plamondon), has described very well in a letter to the Prime Minister the reality of the Frenchspeaking minority in Canada. He also described the reality of the English-speaking minority. Let me quote from his letter:
Anglo-Quebecers get more services than all Canadian minorities combined. In Montreal, for example, English is king in several respects. There are more stores, restaurants and bars where they first address you in English, more magazines published in English, more movie theaters that show films in English, as well as more television and radio stations that broadcast in English. Proportionally, there are more schools and hospitals serving the English community than the Francophone majority itself! And while over 50 per cent of Francophones outside Quebec do not have access to French schools, there is not a single Anglo-Quebecer who cannot be educated in his own language if he so desires!
May 2, 1989

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Richelieu talks about collective rights that must prevail over individual rights as far as language is concerned. As I said before, it is for that very reason, Madam Speaker, that it is up to the National Assembly to decide on the appropriate measures to protect that Francophone minority which represents only 3 per cent of French speakers in North America.
If the Quebec National Assembly decided to implement the measures provided for in article 59(1), I would accept their decision without reservation. But, Madam Speaker, the motion of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace would force Quebecers to accept that principle.
Madam Speaker, I think the linguistic priority in Canada today should be to enforce the right of Francophones outside Quebec, for example in British Columbia or in other provinces, to be educated in their own language. That right is guaranteed by article 23 in the Constitution but, for many Francophones outside Quebec, it is only a dream.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace, on his tenacity and for giving us another opportunity to discuss that important question. But, Madam Speaker, speaking for myself, I would insist on the preservation not of a minority which is already the most privileged in Canada but of the French fact throughout the country.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 PRPOSED AMENDMENT-DELETION OF ARTICLE 59
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the motion under consideration urges this House to ask the Government to initiate an amendment to the Constitution so that Quebec might agree to delete article 59 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which deals with the application of some minority language education guarantees in Quebec.
I will not raise the issue here of whether the anglophone minority in Quebec is well or poorly served as far as English language education is concerned or whether its rights guaranteed by article 23 of the Charter are properly recognized or not. I will also resist the temptation to compare the situation in Quebec with that in the other Canadian provinces.
Neither will I get into a technical debate on the way to amend article 59 of the Charter nor whether Parliament should take the initiative of such an amendment. Never-
Constitution Act
theless, I will say this: however one interprets Parliament's role in deleting article 59, one fact remains-Quebec will have to take a stand.
Now the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace knows very well that successive governments in the National Assembly since the Constitution was repatriated have come out against any participation in constitutional discussions with the rest of the country until an agreement is reached to rectify Quebec's isolation as a result of the 1981 constitutional agreement.
This position of Quebec is why the constitutional reform process in Canada has been blocked since 1982. The failure of negotiations on constitutional matters affecting native people is an example of this.
Aware that Quebec must be heard and the wounds of 1982 healed, the ten provincial premiers agreed in August 1986 to make repatriating Quebec their constitutional priority. This commitment was repeated by all, including the federal Government, at the annual First Ministers' Conference held in Vancouver in November 1986. All agreed to deal first with Quebec's concerns and to postpone all other constitutional issues to a second round of negotiations. This commitment of all governments led to the Meech Lake Accord in June 1987.
To try to open new constitutional negotiations, as the Hon. Member suggests-and with Quebec, to boot- would amount to asking the federal Government to betray its commitment to deal with Quebec's demands first and to postpone other matters until later. Moreover, such an action by the House could be perceived as outright provocation, because it is more than likely that Quebec will refuse to deal with constitutional issues until the Meech Lake Accord is ratified.
Finally, if the Hon. Member is really serious about strengthening minority language education rights he will agree there is a better way to do it. Ratifying the Meech Lake Accord, which acknowledges the linguistic duality as a basic characteristic of the federation, will make it possible to proceed with the constitutional reform, and Canadians will then be in a position to concentrate their efforts on other changes during the annual gatherings of First Ministers which are already provided for under Meech Lake.
It so happens that the federal Government is firmly committed to putting the issue of stronger minority language education rights on the agenda of the first conference after ratification of the Accord.

May 2, 1989
Constitution Act
Here is the Prime Minister's message conveyed last March to linguistic minorities and made public in Quebec by the Association of Quebec Regional English Media:

By allowing Quebec to return to the constitutional table, the Accord will enable us to continue our efforts to improve further the situation of our linguistic minorities. The Government of Canada is committed to address, among other things, the strenghtening of constitutional language rights in their broadest context at the first annual conference following proclamation of the Accord.

On the same occasion Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations Senator Lowell Murray went even further and stated:

These discussions could help clarify, among other matters. Section 23 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms on minority language education rights.

This commitment was repeated on a number of occasions and was given even more solemn currency in the Speech from the Throne. I quote the relevant words:
With Quebec at the table as a willing participant, future constitutional development-including the important issues of Senate reform, of aboriginal and linguistic rights, of roles and responsibilities in relation to fisheries, and of ways to strengthen the Charter of Rights and Freedoms-will become possible and will be a priority of the Government.
That, Madam Speaker, is the gist of my message. Strengthening the right of official language minorities is already slated for the constitutional discussions which will come on the heels of the Meech Lake Accord ratification. Both Quebec's Anglophone minority and Francophone minorities elsewhere in Canada stand to benefit from these discussions.
In any event, adopting the motion now before the House might be construed as a denial of our promise to respond first to Quebec's constitutional requests, prove to be detrimental to the Meech Lake Accord, and seriously undermine the gains the minorities would certainly achieve under the agreement.
Madam Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) will understand my position. In the interest both of Francophones outside Quebec and of Anglophones in Quebec, I urge the House to keep my remarks in mind during the consideration of the motion now under study.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the proposed resolution leads us to examine the constitutionnal guarantees concerning minority language educational rights. As we know, these guarantees are defined in section 23 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms enacted in 1982. The Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) calls upon the Government to amend the Charter and calls upon Quebec to do the same.
I will not discuss the possible response Quebec may give to such a request. However, I would remind you of the will of that Province to deal first and foremost with the question of Meech Lake, and of the Federal Government's commitment and that of all other Governments

May 2, 1989
Constitution Act
to wait for a second round of constitutionnal negotiations before passing to other questions. Besides, I doubt the Hon. Member's motion distinguishes between the first and second rounds of discussions.
In substance, I would say that section 59 is only one aspect of the problem concerning the right to education in the language of the minority. Most Canadians would say that the real problem lies in the difficulty Frenchspeaking Canadians outside Quebec encounter when tiying to have their Provincial Government respect the rights guaranteed them by the Charter in that matter.
Quoting a study made for the Commissioner of Official Languages, the newspaper La Presse of March 6 stated that in English-speaking provinces, only 56 per cent of children aged 6 to 17 who have a right to schooling in French under section 23 of the Charter actually do receive that education. On the other hand, in Quebec, all young people from 6 to 17 entitled to education in English get it, that is 121,513 students.
Among mainly English-speaking provinces, only in New-Brunswick and Ontario do we see more than half the children entitled to instruction in French under section 23 attend French schools. The proportion is 78.4 per cent in New Brunswick. In Ontario, 68.4 per cent of the children with a constitutional right to French schooling attend French schools. Just the same, these figures reflect a major effort on the part of these provinces' Governments over the past fifteen years in the area of minority schooling.
In the other Canadian provinces, the proportion of children with a right to French schooling who attend French schools does not exceed 12.2 per cent. For that matter, it is 7.3 per cent in Alberta and 5.3 per cent in the Northwest Territories.
These figures clearly illustrate one of the major flaws of our Charter in the area of educational rights. It is found in Section 23(3)(a) which expressly provides that the right of Canadian citizens to have their children receive instruction in the language of the minority.
applies wherever in the provinces the number of children of
citizens who have such a right is sufficient to warrant the provision
of them out of public funds of minority language instruction.
That is the infamous "wherever the number warrants" clause which has been so much discredited by all Francophones outside Quebec since 1982.
Under this clause, several provinces with English speaking majorities have been able to limit and continue to limit the instruction services provided to their minorities. In several cases, their French speaking minorities have had to spend a lot of money and wait quite a long time to appeal to the courts to have their needs for French teaching institutions recognized on a case per case basis. As a matter of fact, there were appeal procedures instituted in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
The situation in Quebec is altogether different. That province has never tried to benefit from this law in Section 23 to deny its English speaking minority its right to receive instruction in its own language, no matter the number of pupils or their distribution over the territory.
This situation caused newspaperman Don MacPher-son to write in an article published on March 1st in the Montreal Gazette the following statement, and I quote:

Quebec respects the spirit as well as the letter of the Charter on minority education -In Quebec, the number that warrants a minority language education is one.

To make his point, Mr. MacPherson indicated that the School Board of the Lower North Shore operates an English school with two teachers for a total enrolment of fourteen pupils. He indicated also that half of the $40 million which the Quebec Government allocates to support small schools goes to the English sector.
And Mr. McPherson to conclude, and I quote:

Wouldn't it be a neat trick if, in the next round of constitutional negotiations, Quebec challenged the other provinces to follow its example-and proposed the abolition of the 'where numbers warrant' clause?

If the House is to deal with minority language educational rights, should it not address this side of Section 23? The elimination of the "where numbers warrant" clause is one of the resolutions which the Liberal Party of Canada adopted during its 1986 Convention. Yet, I do not believe that matter of the Section 59 was mentioned there.
May 2, 1989

The Hon. Member's Party voted also in favour of the minority language educational right being defined to include the right to administer these institutions.
The current situation has again compelled minority groups to appeal to the courts to have this right recognized, especially in Ontario. And this other amendment to Section 23 would have the support of the Quebec Government, of Francophones outside Quebec and even Alliance Quebec. Other such reforms might be looked into.
Things may not be easy for the Quebec English speaking minority. According to the last report tabled by the Official Languages Commissioner, small English speaking communities outside Montreal are having difficulties getting provincial services in their own language, while the English speaking community is suffering from under-representation in the Quebec public service. But we can see progress has been made.
With Bill 142, Quebec is trying to make social and health services in English more readily in most of its regions.
Following the new Official Languages Act, the federal government is discussing with Quebec the possibility of increasing federal funding in that area.
With regard to education, Quebec's seventh English CEGEP opened in Hull in October.
Quebec has also tried once more to change its education system in order to create school boards based on language instead of denomination.
As seen in the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages, several opinion leaders, both French and English-speaking, acknowledged that a system based on language criteria would be more suited to the needs of a declining minority group scattered throughout the province, by bringing together the resources of both Catholic and Protestant English schools.
Such a system would also encourage parents to take part in the management of their children schools.
This reform however will not be possible before the courts rule on its constitutionality. Under section 93 of the Constitution Act of 1867, the Quebec school system must respect the rights of individuals to denominational schools. So, we might not be able to bring English-Catholic and English-Protestant students in the same
Constitution Act
schools even if everyone agrees that would be beneficial to minorities.
So here is another constitutional reform that the Hon. Member and this House could tackle if we had to deal with minority language educational rights. I would go as far as to say that it could be very difficult to support such a partial and isolated reform as proposed by the Hon. Member without considering also the application of the legislation where numbers warrant, the rights of institutions to manage their own affairs as will as Section 93, specially in view of the relative viability of the educational situation of the minority in Quebec compared to the situation in other provinces. The francophone minorities outside Quebec could find it insulting if the House gave in to the Hon. Member's request without any concern about the more urgent problems facing thousands of children and parents.
Madam Speaker, I hope the House will give proper consideration to my remarks.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the short time that is left I would like to support the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand). The purpose of his motion is to give support to the principle of attempting to right an historic wrong. I believe it is a noble privilege and duty to be able to fight for the right to correct that wrong.
Rights are rights, when one is English-speaking or French-speaking anywhere across this land. I want my grandchildren educated in French here in Ontario. If they choose to return to Quebec, which I hope they do, and if they choose to have their children educated in English, which I hope they will not, they should still have that right to choice. The whole point is the right to choice-not whether one is English-speaking or Frenchspeaking in Quebec, but the right to make an enlightened choice.
If I were today making an enlightened choice I would choose to go to school in French in Quebec. But do not impose it on me, Madam Speaker. That is the point behind the motion to abrogate Section 59 of the Constitution Act. No Constitution should have an exclusion based on one's language of birth or one's language of choice. It should be an option that everyone should be allowed to take.

May 2, 1989
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-THE BUDGET-CUT-BACKS IN FUNDING-SOCIAL PROGRAM-CUT IN FUNDING
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-THE BUDGET-CUT-BACKS IN FUNDING-SOCIAL PROGRAM-CUT IN FUNDING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last November, in the middle of the election campaign, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) speaking in St. John's, Newfoundland said the following, and I am quoting from the St. John's Evening Telegram: "The federal Government has no plans to make changes to the Unemployment Insurance Program, Trade Minister John Crosbie said Thursday. It is complete nonsense, he replied to questioning by reporters at the Hotel Newfoundland following a Progressive Conservative rally for Prime Minister Brian Mulroney".
It went on to state the following: "Mr. Crosbie said he asked the Prime Minister about the report, and he said, no, the Government has no plan to make changes to the program. You're damn right I asked him", that is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) "about it, and he said, no. No one is planning any changes in the Unemployment Insurance Program, said the Minister for International Trade".
That was last November when the Minister for International Trade, a senior Minister in this Government, said that under no circumstances would there be changes or cuts in the Unemployment Insurance Program. Well here we are in the month of April with two serious cuts and changes to the program.
On April 11, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) announced the redirection of $1.3 billion in the Unemployment Insurance Program to other programs. While $500 million was redirected to improvements in the Unemployment Insurance Program, $800 million was taken away from benefits altogether and redirected to training, to consultation and to labour market planning, things which had always been paid for out of general tax revenue and never paid for with the contributions made by workers and employers to cover themselves during periods of unemployment.
We condemned those changes announced by the Minister because, first of all, they left the unemployed with less coverage during his or her period of unemployment. Second, because they shifted the burden of the unemployed to the provinces, it would be the provinces that would have to help pay for the rent and groceries of those workers during the period of unemployment when they were not covered by unemployment insurance.
Third, we condemned the program because the Government proposed using unemployment insurance money to finance training which is a regressive and inequitable method of financing training. We are all in favour of training, but that is not the way to pay for it.
Finally, we criticized the program because there was no assurance that once trained or retrained that there would be jobs for these workers whether they lived in Summerside, Prince Edward Island or Portage la Prairie. What is the use of training if you do not associate it with an effective program for regional development and for full employment?
We criticize the program for all those things. That was on April 11, when very serious changes were made. Then again last week on April 27 in the Budget, we have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announcing that the Government of Canada will withdraw all its financing of the Unemployment Insurance Program. They are going to take out the $1.9 billion that they "paid in" last year. They are going to leave the financing of the program entirely to workers and to employers. In the past, this has
May 2, 1989

been a three-way financing program. Now the Government of Canada is getting out and leaving the financing entirely to workers and to their employers.
What are we to conclude from all this? We conclude that first of all government Members are attacking the deficit that they have referred to time after time. They are attacking it on the backs of the unemployed. Second, they are attempting to build a level playing field to facilitate free trade with the United States which they said during the election campaign would not be necessary.
I have asked for answers. I have asked for the Government to justify these cuts in unemployment insurance. I have asked how many workers will lose unemployment insurance and to what extent. I have asked the Government to tell us in what region are these workers who would have their unemployment insurance cut. I received no answers.
I asked how these workers who would have their unemployment insurance cut would pay for their rent and groceries. Will the Government let the provinces carry the burden, or will it give them additional money?
Finally, I asked the Minister to justify pulling out the government financing of this program. How does the Government justify pulling out from the financing of this program when the Government of Canada has been helping with the financing since 1941, when it started? We will now have a system that is set adrift and left to the workers and their employers to pay for.
I hope we get some answers to these questions, not for myself and the Liberal Party, but for the people of Canada, who are very concerned about this.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-THE BUDGET-CUT-BACKS IN FUNDING-SOCIAL PROGRAM-CUT IN FUNDING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that the Progressive Conservative government has kept its promise not to reduce its assistance to the unemployed in view of the fact that the purpose of the measures announced by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDou-gall) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is to assist people who lose their jobs. Ten percent of unemploy-
Adjournment Debate
ment insurance funds will be applied to the training and retraining of these people. This goes to show that this government keeps its promises.
It is true that, on January 1 1990, employers and employees alone will contribute to unemployment insurance and that the premium will increase by 30 cents for employees and by 42 cents for employers. But it is also true that these will be the lowest premiums paid over the past six years. The Progressive Conservative government has kept its promise.
We must also keep in mind, in relation to unemployment insurance and to all other programs, the enormous deficit created by the former Liberal government. As we have repeatedly mentioned both in the Budget's speech and elsewhere, Madam Speaker, the Government has agreed, should Canadians be faced again with difficult years such as those they experienced in 1980, 1981 and 1982, to contribute to the fund if it should deem it inapropriate to increase the premiums and preferable to allow the unemployment insurance fund deficit to grow, to meet the needs and expectations of both employers and employees.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I should like to emphasize, for the information of the Hon. Member who made these comments, that the Unemployment Insurance Program has been amended for the purpose of improving the economic welfare of Canada, its employees and employers. These amendments have nothing whatever to do with the free trade issue.
You will remember that during the last election campaign, the opposition tried in vain to scare people both in Quebec and the rest of Canada. We are standing behind the statements we made then: There are programs in Canada. There are social programs in Canada which are and will remain different from those in the United States. We have our own programs and we are determined, as a Progressive Conservatine Government, to continue these programs for the well being of and a better quality of life for all Canadian men and woman. Such is the purpose of the amendements to the Unemployment Insurance Program. To conclude, Madam Speaker, I hope that my hon. friend has finally come to realize that we must work for the future of Canada and not try to jeopardize it all the time.

May 2, 1989
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-DEVELOPMENT OF WELLAND CANAL LANDS-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC MEETINGS
PUBLIC WORKS-DEVELOPMENT OF WELLAND CANAL LANDS-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC MEETINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Public Works Canada and the Welland Canal Development Board presented its final report, entitled "The Old Welland Canal-A Land Use/Marketing Review", at a press conference on April 18, 1989. On April 211 asked the Minister if he had read the report. I have read the report and have come to certain conclusions. I will also quote rather extensively from a very talented and far-sighted Welland city planner by the name of Stan Neatheiy.
My position on this document, indeed on what to do with the Welland Canals themselves, is unequivocal. I believe that these lands should be in the hands of the people of Canada and that not one square inch should ever be sold. Perhaps there could be long-term leases, but not one square inch should be sold. In my opinion, the members of the present board are in the majority pro-development and pro-privatization. I believe that for the majority of the men and women on this board the almighty dollar is more important than the needs and desires of the people of my riding.
With regard to the recommendations the report recommends developing 175 acres of Crown lands, and these are divided into 13 "opportunity areas" along both sides of the central and northern sections of the old canal. These lands are now an open space and some of them are already developed as park land.
Some of the recommendations I agree with. The opportunities presented include a camp ground, a golf course and an old building being changed into a restaurant. I agree with these. However, I want all Hon. Members to know that I am unalterably opposed to the building of a hotel, 135 prestige single, detached housing lots and 40 condominium townhouse lots. Some of these are extending from the service road to the top of the canal bank. Others extend from the service road down to the embankment in order to provide required minimum lot depths in compliance with city zoning by-laws.
Some 63,500 square feet of retail commercial space for small shops alongside the old canal are proposed in the downtown area immediately north of the Main Street
bridge. I disagree with this. I believe we could use the shops that are already there, update them and let the present merchants benefit from any development.
The land area proposed for sale for development represents a substantial amount of the total Crown land holdings alongside the old canal north of Broadway Avenue. It is suggested that the Crown retain the remaining smaller land areas along the canal and Merritt Island.
An emphasis in the report is that public access, including the current system of walkways and bikeways, will be maintained along the entire length of the canal "to the extent that already exists" and that "maintaining public access has been established to be of primary importance in meeting this objective". However, specific opportunity area plans presented in other sections of the report show development to the top of the canal bank. In these instances it is difficult to understand how this objective is to be achieved.
To elaborate, opportunity area E-3, lands between Chippawa Street and the canal water south of Thorold Road and across from Notre Dame Secondary School is shown to be developed either as 25 single or 40 townhouse residential building lots. The accompanying map which I have studied quite carefully shows the boundary of the area slated for sale and development approximating 13 feet from the water's edge. However, the average horizontal distance from the top of the bank to the canal water's edge is 30 feet on a steep slope. Accordingly, it is difficult to understand just how "public access has been maintained throughout to a minimum depth of 33 feet".
Further, to maintain a public access area of 33 feet wide in opportunity area E-3 would take up half the land area to be sold and developed. The report estimates total development costs for all the opportunity areas to approximate $36.2 million-$35.2 million in construction and $1 million in servicing. In addition, one section of the report estimates that the development of the canal lands would generate $115.9 million in direct and indirect expenditures. It estimates that 2,680 new jobs would result from the development of the canal lands: 1,456 direct and the remainder indirect. However, a later section of the report states that total direct and indirect expenditures would equal $81.6 million, and only 1,882 direct and indirect new jobs would result. These are significant discrepancies, which should be explained.
May 2, 1989

Although the report did not specify the types of jobs generated by the canal lands development of the various opportunity areas, it is believed that a major portion of these jobs would be construction related. I believe many of these jobs would be seasonal.
The estimated taxation impact of the development of the canal lands is estimated in one area at $491,625 per year; but in a later area it is $381,375, a discrepancy of 22 per cent.
To summarize, it seems to me: (1) that sufficient public access alongside the old canal is not guaranteed; (2) that a significant amount of existing Crown parklands alongside the old canal would be sold to private developers; (3) that there appear to be discrepancies in the amount of dollars that would be generated in the local economy as a result of the proposed sale and development of the canal lands.
I denounce this report as being unacceptable to the majority of the people in the Welland-St. Catharines- Thorold riding. Surely it is not worth anywhere near the $30,000 it cost to produce it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-DEVELOPMENT OF WELLAND CANAL LANDS-REQUEST FOR PUBLIC MEETINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1973 the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority completed the construction of a bypass canal around the city of Welland. Subsequently, in 1974 the Seaway Authority transferred to Public Works Canada the ownership and management of 317 hectares of residual canal and adjacent federal lands that bisect the city center. The property consisted of 45 hectares of water, 150 hectares of spoil piles, and a 45-hectare island between the canal and the river, known as Merritt Island, with the canal banks varying in width from 20 metres to 200 metres.
In the fall of 1979 the Minister of Public Works visited Welland and later appointed a local citizens advisory committee, the Welland Canal Advisory Group, to advise on the development and long-term management of the lands.
In 1984 the advisory group was replaced by the Welland Canal Parkway Development Board, with a revised mandate. The board was charged with advising the Minister on matters pertaining to the redevelopment of the lands using alternative sources of funding, including private-sector financing and entrepreneurship, and developing a long-term management and operating plan
Adjournment Debate
for the canal lands that would best represent the interests of the Crown and the municipality.
Since 1976 the department has spent over $20 million in capital, operation, and maintenance grants in lieu of taxes. Much of the area is fully landscaped and actively maintained, consistent with the standards practised by the National Capital Commission and the Niagara Parks Commission. In 1988 the department spent approximately $350,000 on operation and maintenance and $465,000 on grants in lieu of taxes.
In a news conference on April 15, 1988, the Chairman of the Welland Canal Parkway Development Board, the Mayor of Welland, and the local Members of Parliament announced the approval of the Minister of Public Works to commission a consultant to undertake an independent land use study. Specifically, the study was to identify potential recreation and residential and commerical land development opportunities supported by economic viability. The final report was submitted to the department on April 14, 1989. A news conference was held on April 18 at which the Member of Parliament for Erie (Mr. Fretz) announced the completion of the study.
The study has identified a number of potential recreational, residential, and commercial opportunities along the waterway that could complement adjacent land uses.
Preliminary economic analysis reveals that some of these are viable as short-term options, that is for three to five years, while others would be safer ventures in the medium and long term, that is from five to ten years respectively. In addition, new employment, additional tax revenue and development money could be generated for the City of Welland.
In the upcoming weeks, Public Works Canada will be soliciting comments from the citizens of Welland through information booths and special briefings to various local interest groups.
The Department has also extended an invitation to the City of Welland to establish a working group between the city and Public Works Canada. The purpose of the group will be to address each of the opportunities identified in the consultant's report and develop a specific action plan which will benefit the City and the federal Government. May I say again that the disposition of these lands will be made in full consultation with the people of Welland.

May 2, 1989
Adjournment Debate
The Regional Municipality of Niagara, with the assistance of the Canada-Ontario Tourism Subsidiary Agreement, has also just completed a study of the whole Welland corridor of which the Public Works lands is a part. The object of their study was to look at the tourism potential and the opportunities of the area.
The Minister gave an assurance in this House on April 21 that the consultants engaged by Public Works Canada were hired only to identify potential development opportunities. The Minister emphasized the word "potential" and gave the Hon. Member for Welland-St. Catharines (Mr. Parent) the assurance that there will be full consultation with the City.
