subtopic: IMMIGRATION - LEBANON - PLIGHT OF REFUGEES-CONSULAR SERVICES IN CYPRUS-UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSION ON REFUGEES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY MEETING
IMMIGRATION - LEBANON - PLIGHT OF REFUGEES-CONSULAR SERVICES IN CYPRUS-UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSION ON REFUGEES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY MEETING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to address this full House this evening on a question that I had an opportunity of asking the Minister and the Government back on April 20.
The question pertained to the issue of Lebanon, which for the last 15 years has never seen as fierce fighting and as fierce an escalation in the war torn zone, producing very horrible results and producing refugees and homeless people in a number that is indeed very worrisome.
We in the Liberal Party had asked repeatedly in the House both the Minister responsible for immigration and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to establish, at the very earliest, a full consular immigration operation in Cyprus, because the very large and proud Lebanese Canadian community in this country wanted to extend an invitation or a sponsorship to families and friends back in Lebanon who wish to escape the very horrific scenes we see on our television sets day in and day out.
The problem was the inability and the inaccessibility of people in Lebanon to get to a Canadian office in order to complete the necessary applications and forms.
We have a full operation in Damascus, Syria, but because Syria is one of the antagonists in the war we could hardly imagine whether people, particularly of the
Christian faith, would venture into Damascus, Syria. Therefore, we had asked for a full consular operation in Cyprus.
The Government finally responded to those calls by saying that it was going to send one official to Cyprus in order to process those applications.
It is our contention that one official is not only unfair but indeed misleading if we are to look at the long-term solution. At the very least, we are in need of a temporaiy full operation so that those who wish to come to Canada and elsewhere may have a hope and a chance of doing so. It is our contention that sending one official is clearly not addressing the magnitude of the problem.
On a secondary aspect we asked this Government to initiate an emergency meeting through the offices of the United Nations High Commission on Refugees which informed me that it only had a skeleton staff of three people in Lebanon to try to deal with the magnitude of the problem.
We suggested in Question Period, because we are members of the UNHCR, that clearly Canada can exercise some leadership and ask the UNHCR to beef up its representation in Lebanon so that not only Canada will try to help those who wish to flee and to reunite families in this country, but that other countries across the globe through the efforts of the UNHCR can share and participate in removing people from a place in the world that is completely tortured and, as I said at the outset, has seen fighting not previously seen for the last 15 years.

Therefore, Madam Speaker, I hope the Government will offer a real solution to Lebanese-Canadians because a single immigration officer in Lebanon is neither a true nor a fair solution. Our party thinks that we need a full-time immigration consular operation staffed with six or seven employees who could answer inquiries from parents, relatives and people in Canada who are willing to work but who want to leave Lebanon because of the terrible situation experienced by everybody in that country today. I think that the Canadian Government could continue to play a very significant role by setting an example for other countries to follow. But I think having a single immigration official, in Cyprus for example, to process applications is simply not a real solution.
May 2, 1989

Therefore, Madam Speaker, I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will propose a fairer and more efficient solution and I hope to get that answer today.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: IMMIGRATION - LEBANON - PLIGHT OF REFUGEES-CONSULAR SERVICES IN CYPRUS-UNITED NATIONS HIGH COMMISSION ON REFUGEES-REQUEST FOR EMERGENCY MEETING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know Lebanon quite well. When I first went to Lebanon it was the jewel of the Mediterranean. It was a great place for a vacation. It was a banking centre. After visiting other countries it was great to get to Lebanon. The last time I was there I think our aircraft was allowed to land and refuel and we had to take off immediately. We could not even go into the city.
I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the Hon. Minister of State for Employment and Immigration (Mrs. Vezina) to the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) on April 20.
Canada has had special measures in effect for victims of unrest in Lebanon for some time. This special program for Lebanese, which remains in effect, allows relatives in the assisted relative category to be sponsored for immigration to Canada under a relaxed criteria. In 1988 over 800 Lebanese were admitted to Canada under this program. Since 1973 we have admitted over 15,000. As the situation in Lebanon remains unpredictable, it will be monitored by officials of the Department of External Affairs and adjustments to immigration services will be made accordingly. In other words, if we find it is getting more difficult and there are more applications we will adjust our people there accordingly.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees has not considered this issue a refugee movement at this stage. We are in contact with his representatives in the area.
Adjournment Debate
and this could change. The main immigration office for the area is in Damascus, and continues to provide service to the people from Lebanon who are able to get through. But I can see that is a very difficult thing to get through, particularly if you are a Christian going through the Bekaa Valley to try to get to Damascus.
Similarly, the Canadian visa office in Cyprus has been able to meet the demand for immigration services there. Lor those already outside Lebanon, Canada has an honorary consul in Cyprus and there is presently an immigration officer in Nicosia who is providing immigration services and he has several civilian assistants to help him.
A special courier service has been established between Damascus and Nicosia. Lebanese who have completed visa formalities may collect their immigration visa in either city. A Lebanese may also approach any other Canadian mission in order to apply for immigration under the special Lebanese program.
For the moment, therefore, we believe Canada is providing good service to those who can leave Lebanon and qualify under the terms of the special measures. We shall continue to assess the developments in the event that additional issues emerge and a greater level of service is required.
We thank the Hon. Member for his continued interest in this matter.
